newsitem.title: KENYA: Focus-Kenya halts coffee auctions as supply ebbs.
newsitem.headline: Focus-Kenya halts coffee auctions as supply ebbs.

text.p: Kenya has suspended its weekly coffee export auctions for the next two weeks because of acute shortages, a senior official at the Coffee Board of Kenya (CBK) said on Friday.
CBK official Charles Gatere said in a statement auctions would resume on July 22 and would continue normally after that.
"This is to advise you that due to inadequate supply of coffee, auctions will close for the next two weeks. Auctions will resume on July 22," Gatere told Reuters.

A Kenya Coffee Auctions Ltd official said earlier auctions would probably resume in the last week of the month if there were sufficient coffee for an auction. After that, Kenya would auction coffee twice a month "depending on whether we get any".
But Gatere said, "There has been a misunderstanding. Auctions will certainly resume on the July 22 and will continue normally (every week) from then on."
The Auctions official said they expected two auctions in August, instead of weekly, and supply was not yet determined.

The Auctions official told Reuters in Nairobi: "It is simple. There is no coffee. Like cars or batteries, if you have nothing to sell, you sell nothing." He said it was not known when the coffee supply situation would improve.

Drought that ravaged most growing areas of East Africa from October last year and persisted to March had forced a severe cut in coffee production and coffee reaching the market from farmers was well below earlier predictions, said CBK field monitors.
They added that Kenya had pushed through the auctions as much coffee as it had while global prices for its mild arabicas were high and this had left it with a very tight supply equation.

A trader from a leading coffee house in Nairobi said that coffee from the mid "fly" crop was forecast at just between 20,000 and 25,000 tonnes. An estimated total crop of 70-75,000 tonnes in 1996/97 (Oct/Sept) sounded further bad news for 1997/98 estimates.
The Coffee Board revised its estimate to 78,500 tonnes.
The trader told Reuters, "The Coffee Board had earlier variously forecast a mid crop of 27,000 to 35,000 tonnes and a main crop of 60,000 tonnes. Results from the field negate this."

The trader said that forecasts for the 1997/98 crop would have to start at a conservative 80-85,000 tonnes to factor in the effects of drought. The Coffee Board has previously put that provisional production figure at 100,000 tonnes.
The 1996/97 production figure will be matched against 97,575 in 1995/96 and 95,806 tonnes in 1994/95, according to the CBK.

Traders said that the weekly export auctions normally went into recess in August. But they added that the Coffee Board had informed traders of a possibility of two auctions in that month on the basis of "we will sell whatever it is that we get".

"We are now taking an unusual holiday. If the supply situation continues as it is, it is likely that Kenya will have no coffee to sell in November and December -- because we would have sold all the mid crop by then," a senior trader said.
At this week's export auction on Tuesday, Kenyan premium grades Grade ABs averaged $265 per 50-kg from $317 the previous week and grade AAs averaged $282 from $326.
That compared to record high mid-May prices of $540 per 50 kg FAQ (Fair Average Quality) and $520 for ABs FAQ.
Traders said the coffee beans that had so far reached the market from the mid crop were very light and drought-affected.
Coffee is ranked third behind tourism and tea as a leading foreign exchange earner, according to Treasury figures.
